script.opening: "Thanks. So I've had IBS for years — dodgy stomach, bloating, running to the loo — I've kind of made my peace with it. But I'm SO tired lately, wiped out, and my last blood test apparently showed I'm a bit anaemic. Could you just give me some stronger tablets for the tummy and maybe iron for the tiredness? I haven't got time to be ill, honestly."

facts.text: If asked: since your early twenties. Bloating most days, loose pale stools two or three times a day, cramps. "IBS" was suggested by a GP years ago; you never had tests. No blood in your stools, no black stools.
Exhausted for about six months; falling asleep on the sofa by 8pm. Breathless on stairs.
Lost about half a stone over the past year without trying — "I put it down to being busy." Mouth ulcers on and off. No itchy blistering rash. Periods regular and not heavy.

You eat everything — toast, sandwiches, pasta. You have wondered about cutting out bread because it makes you bloated, but have not yet. If asked: you are happy to keep eating gluten for the test once the reason is explained.
Your sister has type 1 diabetes. Mum has an underactive thyroid. Nobody with coeliac disease that you know of.
Loperamide from the chemist most days. No allergies. Not pregnant.
32, secondary school teacher, head of year. Lives with partner. Rarely drinks, never smoked.
You have quietly been frightened for months that "something is really wrong" — your friend was diagnosed with bowel cancer at 35. Say this only if the doctor asks what worries you.

Brisk and busy; you want a quick prescription. If the doctor suggests it might not be IBS, you are surprised, then interested: "So it might actually have a name?" If they explain the test and why you must keep eating gluten, ask: "So I shouldn't cut out bread then?"

ice.ideas: "It's just my IBS and I'm tired from work."
ice.concerns: Mainly coping at work. Underneath: a fear that something serious has been missed.
ice.expectations: "Stronger tummy tablets and some iron." You are open to tests if they might explain everything.

cues: "I haven't got time to be ill." — say in the opening.
"I've lost a bit of weight, but that's just being busy." — say if weight is asked about.
"My sister's got diabetes — the type 1 kind." — say if family history is asked.

checkpoints.text: Recognises that IRON-DEFICIENCY ANAEMIA with chronic GI symptoms should NOT simply be labelled "IBS" — it is a flag to investigate — and that the cluster (anaemia, fatigue, mouth ulcers, weight loss, autoimmune family history) points to possible COELIAC DISEASE

Arranges COELIAC SEROLOGY correctly: tTG-IgA with total IgA, and crucially advises her to KEEP EATING GLUTEN (gluten in more than one meal a day for at least 6 weeks, NICE NG20) before/at testing — not to cut gluten first, which would make the test unreliable

Investigates the IRON-DEFICIENCY ANAEMIA properly (ferritin/iron studies, diet, menstrual losses) rather than just prescribing iron blindly — oral iron can start alongside the work-up (BSG iron-deficiency anaemia guideline 2021) — and recognises coeliac as a cause (BSG 2021: screen all adults with iron-deficiency anaemia for coeliac disease); plans gastroenterology referral for duodenal biopsy if serology is positive

Knows the implications and associations: untreated coeliac risks anaemia, osteoporosis, subfertility and (rarely) malignancy; associated with type 1 diabetes, autoimmune thyroid disease, dermatitis herpetiformis — so making the diagnosis matters

Reframes from symptom-patching to diagnosis: explains that "IBS" may be the wrong label, that this is testable, and that a positive result means a treatable condition where a gluten-free diet often transforms symptoms — rather than just stronger tablets
Hears the exhaustion and the suppressed "something’s wrong" fear behind the brisk request, and the self-sacrificing pattern; validates it and offers the hope of a treatable, named diagnosis
Avoids dismissiveness (just relabelling/iron) and engages her in finding the cause, checking understanding of the keep-eating-gluten instruction

Safety-nets and follows up: the serology and anaemia work-up plan with the gluten instruction, gastroenterology referral pathway if positive, dietitian involvement for confirmed coeliac, and a follow-up to go through results — finding the diagnosis, not patching the symptoms

worked.txt: "Can I gently challenge something? You’ve carried an ‘IBS’ label for years — but IBS shouldn’t make you anaemic, and now your bloods show you are. That’s an important clue, because it tells me there might be a specific, FINDABLE reason for both the tummy symptoms AND the exhaustion, rather than just ‘your IBS’. I don’t want to keep patching it; I’d like to actually work it out."

"Putting it together — the long tummy troubles, the anaemia, the tiredness, the mouth ulcers, and your sister’s type 1 diabetes — makes me think of a condition called coeliac disease, where the gut reacts to gluten. It’s common, often missed for years under an IBS label, and crucially it’s very treatable once we know."

"There’s one really important thing: the blood test for it only works if you’re STILL eating gluten. So please do NOT cut out bread and pasta before the test — keep eating normally, including gluten, right up to and after the blood test, or we’ll get a false result and have to start again. That catches a lot of people out."

"I also want to look into the anaemia properly rather than just throw iron at it — check your iron stores and why it’s happening, because coeliac is one reason the body doesn’t absorb iron well. If the coeliac test is positive, you’d see a gut specialist for a confirming test, and a dietitian to help with the diet."

"I know you came for stronger tablets and ‘no time to be ill’ — but I think you’ve been quietly worried something’s really wrong, and soldiering on. Here’s the hopeful bit: if this IS coeliac, it’s not something sinister, it’s treatable, and a lot of people feel like a completely different person once they’re off gluten. That could be your energy back."

"So: keep eating gluten, I’ll arrange the coeliac blood test and sort the anaemia work-up, and we’ll go from there — specialist and dietitian if it’s positive. If you get any new alarming symptoms — blood in your stools, ongoing weight loss, severe pain — tell me sooner. Let’s find the actual answer rather than manage a label that might be wrong."

f.learning: A long-standing "IBS" label PLUS iron-deficiency anaemia is a red flag, not a refill request — IBS does not cause iron-deficiency anaemia, and the cluster here (anaemia, fatigue, mouth ulcers, weight loss, a sister with type 1 diabetes — an associated autoimmune condition, not itself a NICE NG20 testing criterion) points to COELIAC DISEASE being missed for years. The examinable clinical point is testing it RIGHT: coeliac serology (tTG-IgA with total IgA) is only reliable while the patient is still eating gluten, so advise her to KEEP eating gluten (in more than one meal a day for at least 6 weeks, NICE NG20) and NOT to cut it before testing; a positive result leads to gastroenterology referral for confirmatory duodenal biopsy, and the iron-deficiency anaemia must be investigated properly rather than blindly treated with iron. Making the diagnosis matters (untreated coeliac risks anaemia, osteoporosis, subfertility and rarely malignancy). The hidden agenda is exhaustion and a suppressed "something’s really wrong" fear behind a self-sacrificing "no time to be ill" request; reframe from symptom-patching to finding the cause, and offer the genuine hope of a treatable, named diagnosis where a gluten-free diet often transforms symptoms.

knowledge.guideline: NICE NG20 (2015) · NICE CG61 (2008, updated 2017) · NICE HTG320 (2013, formerly DG11) · BSG iron-deficiency anaemia guideline (2021)
knowledge.summary: IBS does not cause iron-deficiency anaemia. Years of “IBS” plus iron deficiency, tiredness, mouth ulcers and a little weight loss is coeliac disease until serology says otherwise — tested correctly, while she is still eating gluten.

points.t: NICE CG61: IBS is diagnosed only after the red flags and baseline tests are clear — FBC, ESR/CRP and coeliac serology. Anaemia and unexplained weight loss are among the features that call for further investigation rather than an IBS label.

points.h: Who to test for coeliac disease
points.t: NICE NG20: offer serology to people with persistent unexplained GI symptoms, IBS-type symptoms, unexplained iron, B12 or folate deficiency, unexplained weight loss, prolonged fatigue, severe or persistent mouth ulcers, type 1 diabetes, autoimmune thyroid disease, and first-degree relatives of people with coeliac disease. A sister with type 1 diabetes adds weight to an autoimmune picture but is not in itself a testing criterion.

NICE NG20: first-line is total IgA plus IgA tissue transglutaminase (tTG-IgA); use IgG-based tests if IgA-deficient. The person must eat gluten in more than one meal every day for at least 6 weeks before testing. Advise explicitly not to cut gluten out before the diagnosis is confirmed.

NICE NG20: positive serology → refer to gastroenterology for endoscopic duodenal biopsy, still eating gluten. Do not diagnose coeliac disease in adults on serology alone. After diagnosis: lifelong gluten-free diet, dietitian support, bone health assessment, and assessment for functional hyposplenism with vaccination per the Green Book (pneumococcal where indicated).

points.h: The anaemia in its own right
points.t: BSG 2021: confirm iron deficiency with ferritin, screen all adults with IDA for coeliac disease, ask about menstrual loss and diet, and treat with oral iron while the cause is sought — product and dose per BNF. In premenopausal women, GI investigation is guided by symptoms, age and family history, and offers FIT to adults with iron-deficiency anaemia. Faecal calprotectin (NICE HTG320) helps separate IBD from IBS in adults with lower GI symptoms.

Untreated coeliac disease leads to ongoing malabsorption, anaemia, low bone density and subfertility, and rarely small-bowel lymphoma. A gluten-free diet usually settles symptoms and restores iron, so a named diagnosis is worth far more than stronger antidiarrhoeals.

dg.d: Open question first; let her describe the “IBS”, the tiredness and what the anaemia result meant to her before responding to the tablet request.
Teaching workload, the impact of exhaustion on work and identity, and the “no time to be ill” pattern.
Total IgA plus tTG-IgA while on gluten; ferritin and haematinics; ESR/CRP; faecal calprotectin; abdominal examination at a face-to-face review.
Coeliac disease versus IBD versus menstrual or dietary iron loss; recognises that IBS does not explain iron deficiency.
Asked about rectal bleeding, nocturnal symptoms and weight loss; clear on when this becomes urgent.
Possible coeliac disease under a long IBS label, with iron-deficiency anaemia from malabsorption — shared in plain words.
After open exploration, used closed questions with clear signposting to confirm specific details.
Used information already available in the notes/referral; did not re-ask what was already documented or said.

dg.t: Finishes data gathering in good time
dg.d: History, ICE, psychosocial context and red-flag screen completed by ~6–7 minutes, leaving time for explanation and a shared plan.

cm.d: Keep eating gluten (more than one meal a day, at least 6 weeks); serology; oral iron while investigating; biopsy referral if positive; no escalation of antidiarrhoeals.
Looks for other deficiencies (B12, folate, vitamin D); plans dietitian, bone health and vaccination if coeliac is confirmed.
Results review booked; GI bleeding, further weight loss, severe pain or anaemia symptoms named for earlier contact.

cm.t: Uses psychosocial information in the plan
cm.d: Tailored the plan to the patient’s circumstances, beliefs and practical barriers rather than giving a generic plan.

cm.t: Shares risks and safety of options
cm.d: Explained the benefits and risks of the options clearly, as concrete terms or numbers where possible.
Acknowledged autonomy, capacity, confidentiality, safeguarding and any fitness-to-drive/work or duty-of-care implications relevant to this case.
Moved efficiently through the consultation so all key areas were covered within the time without getting stuck.

ro.d: Picked up “not the person I was”, the weight loss she dismissed and the mouth ulcers she blamed on stress.
Her idea (long-standing IBS plus work), the buried fear that something is really wrong, and her wish for stronger tablets and iron.
Warm, non-judgmental tone; put the patient at ease and showed respect for their perspective.
Opened broadly and let the patient tell their story before narrowing down.
When a cue was offered, stopped and explored the specific concern rather than reassuring superficially and moving on.
Active listening throughout — reflecting, pausing, not interrupting — interested in the patient as a person.
Told the patient why a question, examination or test was being done — transparent reasoning throughout.
Explained the working diagnosis or analysis in plain language the patient could understand.

ro.t: Shares and uses ICE in the plan
ro.d: Addressed the patient’s specific concern — Mainly coping at work. Underneath: a fear that something serious has been missed — directly within the plan, rather than noting it and moving on.
Checked understanding, offered written/follow-up support, asked if anything else was on their mind, agreed next steps.
Clear agenda set early, logical flow from data gathering to management. Did not jump to a plan before gathering enough information.
Explained clinical terms in plain English, or defined them immediately; checked the patient was following.
Noticed and responded to emotional and verbal cues rather than continuing a fixed clinical script.

model.text: Hello Erin, I’m Dr Shah. I can see your blood results, but before I say anything about them — tell me in your own words what’s been going on.
model.why: Open question before the results or the request

model.text: I’ve had IBS for years — bloating, running to the loo, cramps. I’ve made my peace with it. But I’m so tired lately, and the blood test says I’m anaemic. Can I just have some stronger tummy tablets and some iron? I haven’t got time to be ill.

Thank you — that’s clear, and I’ll come back to the tablets and the iron. I’d like to ask a few questions about the tummy and the tiredness, explain what I think the blood test is telling us, and agree a plan. Is that okay?
model.why: Acknowledges her request and sets a shared agenda

model.text: Sure. As long as it’s quick.
Tell me about the tiredness. How is it affecting you, day to day?
model.why: Explores impact rather than accepting “just tired”

model.text: Wiped out. I get home from school and just sit. I’m not the person I was, if I’m honest.
That sounds hard. With the tummy — any blood in your stools, or waking at night to open your bowels?
No blood. Just loose, and a lot of bloating.
Has your weight changed at all? And do you get any mouth ulcers, or any itchy rash?
model.why: Targets the coeliac cluster: weight loss, ulcers, skin

model.text: I’ve lost a bit, but I’m busy, so… And yes, I get mouth ulcers now and then. I thought that was stress.
Does anything like coeliac disease, thyroid problems or diabetes run in the family?
My sister has type 1 diabetes. Nothing else that I know of.
And your periods — would you say they’re heavy? And what’s a normal day of eating for you — plenty of bread, pasta, cereal?
model.why: Other causes of IDA, and confirms she is currently eating gluten

model.text: Nothing out of the ordinary with periods, I don’t think. And I eat normally — toast, sandwiches, pasta. The usual.
You said you’re not the person you were. Has any part of you been wondering whether something more is going on?
model.why: Picks up the cue and gently surfaces the hidden fear

model.text: …Honestly? Yes. I keep telling myself it’s IBS and work, but sometimes I lie awake thinking something’s really wrong with me. I just push it down.
Thank you for saying that. It makes sense after years of feeling like this — and I don’t think you’ve been making a fuss over nothing. I think your body has been telling us something.
model.why: Validates the fear and the self-sacrificing pattern

model.text: Here’s what stands out. IBS doesn’t make people anaemic — and you are. Put that with the tummy symptoms, the tiredness, the mouth ulcers and the weight loss, and I think of a condition called coeliac disease, where the gut reacts to gluten and stops absorbing iron properly.
model.why: IDA is a flag against IBS; names coeliac from the cluster

model.text: Coeliac? I’ve had IBS for years. Nobody’s ever said that.

It’s common and it hides behind an IBS label for years. The good news is it’s a blood test to start with, and if it’s positive a specialist confirms it with a small sample from the gut taken during a camera test.
model.why: Explains serology then biopsy confirmation in adults

model.text: One thing matters more than anything else: the test only works if you keep eating gluten — bread, pasta, cereal in more than one meal every day. Please don’t cut it out before the test, or the result can come back falsely normal. Can you tell me back what I’ve asked you to do?
Keep eating bread and pasta as normal, don’t go gluten-free yet, even if I want to.

Exactly. So the plan I’d suggest: the coeliac blood test with a total antibody level, iron stores and a few other checks, and a stool test that looks for gut inflammation. I’ll also start iron now, because you need it — but alongside finding out why, not instead of it. How does that sound?
model.why: Anaemia work-up plus treatment, not iron alone

model.text: That makes sense. What about stronger tablets for my stomach?

I’d rather not escalate those yet — if this is coeliac disease, stronger tablets only mask it. Use your loperamide sparingly if you need it for school. If the test is positive, you’d see a gut specialist and a dietitian, and many people feel like a different person once they’re properly gluten-free.
model.why: Negotiates the request honestly and offers hope

model.text: That would be amazing. I’d love my energy back.
And while we wait, is there anything at work that would help — even just not taking on extra this term?
model.why: Tailors the plan to her “no time to be ill” pattern

model.text: Maybe. I always say yes to everything.

If you notice blood in your stools, black stools, weight dropping further, severe pain, or feeling breathless or faint, contact us sooner rather than waiting. I’ll book a call to go through the results in about two weeks.
model.why: Specific safety-net and a booked follow-up

model.text: Okay. Thank you — I came in for tablets and I feel like I’ve actually been listened to.
So: keep eating gluten, bloods and stool test this week, iron started, and a call in two weeks. Anything we haven’t covered?
No, that’s everything.

social.t: A teacher who says yes to everything and has “no time to be ill”. Exhaustion is affecting her work and sense of self; the plan must fit a school timetable, not add guilt.
If confirmed, a lifelong gluten-free diet affects shopping, cost, eating out and school meals. Dietitian input and label-reading skills decide whether it works.

legal.t: If fatigue or investigations affect her work, a fit note can suggest adjustments (for example altered duties) rather than full absence. Coeliac disease can be a disability under the Equality Act 2010 where its effects are substantial and long-term — relevant only if symptoms persist.

professional.t: A diagnosis recorded years ago is a working hypothesis, not a fact. New results that don’t fit — iron deficiency here — are a prompt to re-examine it (GMC Good Medical Practice 2024: good clinical care).
Escalating antidiarrhoeals or giving iron without investigating the cause would treat numbers and symptoms, not the patient. Document the reasoning and the gluten advice.

community.t: Coeliac UK (information, food directory, local groups); community pharmacy for iron counselling; practice dietitian or local dietetic service after diagnosis. Gluten-free food on prescription varies by area.

redFlags: Iron-deficiency anaemia with bowel symptoms — not explained by IBS
Unintentional weight loss, rectal bleeding, nocturnal diarrhoea — investigate rather than label
Symptoms of significant anaemia: breathlessness, chest pain, near-faints — earlier review
psychosocial: Impact of fatigue on teaching and on how she sees herself
The “no time to be ill” pattern that has kept her normalising symptoms
Practical barriers to tests and to a future diet change
ice: Idea: “It’s my IBS and work tiredness”
Concern: a buried fear that something is really wrong, pushed down for years
Expectation: stronger tummy tablets and iron, quickly

playbook.diagnosis: Be honest that the label may be wrong: “IBS doesn’t cause iron deficiency. With your symptoms, the ulcers and the weight loss, I want to test for coeliac disease — and I’d like to find the cause rather than keep treating the symptoms.”
playbook.diagnosisLay: “Think of the lining of your gut as a thick carpet that soaks up iron and nutrients. In coeliac disease, gluten wears the carpet thin, so iron slips through. The blood test looks for the body’s reaction to gluten — which is why you need to keep eating it until we’ve tested.”

management.reflectIce: “You’ve been quietly worried something is really wrong and kept going anyway. I think you were right to wonder — and the good news is that what I’m looking for is very treatable.”
management.psychosocial: Work with her pace: one set of tests this week, iron started, a results call booked. Invite her to take something off her plate at work while this is sorted.
sharedPlan: Total IgA plus tTG-IgA while eating gluten in more than one meal a day (at least 6 weeks); ferritin, B12, folate, ESR/CRP; faecal calprotectin
Oral iron now, product and dose per BNF, while the cause is sought
Positive serology → gastroenterology for duodenal biopsy; dietitian, bone health and vaccination review if confirmed
safetyNet: Rectal bleeding or black stools, further weight loss, severe pain, breathlessness or faintness → contact the practice promptly
Results review in about two weeks; do not start a gluten-free diet until told the diagnosis is confirmed

pitfalls.intro: This station is failed by doctors who treat the request rather than the patient: a stronger tablet, some iron, and a diagnosis nobody checked. The marks sit in spotting that the numbers don’t fit the label, and in testing correctly.

items.fail: Accepting “IBS” and prescribing a stronger antispasmodic or antidiarrhoeal.
items.why: IBS does not cause iron-deficiency anaemia; NICE CG61 requires anaemia and weight loss to be investigated. “Management plan not in line with current UK best practice.”
items.fix: Say it out loud: “IBS doesn’t make people anaemic — so I want to look for a cause.” Then test for coeliac disease.

items.fail: Suggesting a trial of gluten-free diet before any blood test.
items.why: NICE NG20: the person must eat gluten in more than one meal a day for at least 6 weeks before testing; going gluten-free makes serology and biopsy unreliable.
items.fix: Give the instruction clearly and check it with teach-back: “Tell me what I’ve asked you to do about bread and pasta.”

items.fail: Ordering tTG-IgA alone, or diagnosing coeliac disease on serology and starting the diet.
items.why: Total IgA is needed to avoid a false negative in IgA deficiency, and adults need biopsy confirmation (NICE NG20).
items.fix: “A blood test for the antibody and your total antibody level; if it’s positive, a specialist confirms it with a small sample from the gut.”

items.fail: Missing “I’m not the person I was” and moving straight to tests.
items.why: “Does not identify or respond to the patient’s cues.” Her hidden agenda is a long-suppressed fear, and it is what makes her engage with the plan.
items.fix: Pause: “Has part of you been wondering whether something more is going on?” Then validate before explaining.

items.fail: Dismissing her request flatly — “No, you don’t need stronger tablets.”
items.why: Refusing without explanation reads as paternalistic and loses her trust in the investigation plan.
items.fix: Explain why: “If this is coeliac disease, stronger tablets would only hide it. Let’s find the cause — and I’ll treat your iron today.”

items.fail: Closing with “we’ll ring you with the results” and nothing else.
items.why: Non-specific safety-netting and no defined follow-up are standard failing feedback.
items.fix: Name the red flags (bleeding, black stools, weight loss, faintness), book the results call, and summarise the plan in one sentence.

timeMap.d: She opens with a fixed request. Let her finish, then ask about the tiredness — that is where the story is.
Red flags (blood, nocturnal symptoms, weight), coeliac cluster (ulcers, rash, family autoimmunity), periods and diet — and confirm she is eating gluten now.
Surface the buried “something’s really wrong” fear. Validate it before you explain anything.
IBS doesn’t cause iron deficiency. Name coeliac. The keep-eating-gluten instruction with teach-back. Serology, anaemia work-up, iron now, biopsy if positive.
GI red flags named, results call booked, summary and a question to share the floor.

wordPics.fail: Relabels it as IBS, prescribes a stronger antispasmodic and iron, and closes; never connects anaemia with the bowel symptoms; advises a trial of gluten-free diet “to see if it helps” before testing; misses the exhaustion and fear.
wordPics.pass: Recognises that iron deficiency doesn’t fit IBS; arranges coeliac serology with total IgA and tells her to keep eating gluten; checks for red flags; starts iron while investigating; books results follow-up.
wordPics.exc: All of the above, plus: draws out the suppressed fear and the “no time to be ill” pattern and answers both; uses teach-back on the gluten instruction; explains biopsy confirmation and dietitian support; offers the genuine hope of a treatable diagnosis; she leaves feeling heard, not dismissed.

avoid.dont: “Try cutting out gluten for a few weeks and see if you feel better.”
avoid.instead: “Please keep eating gluten in more than one meal a day until we’ve done the test — otherwise it can come back falsely normal.”
avoid.why: A gluten-free trial before serology is the classic error and can delay the diagnosis by months.

avoid.dont: “Your IBS is flaring — let’s try a stronger tablet.”
avoid.instead: “IBS doesn’t make people anaemic, so I think there’s a findable reason for all of this.”
avoid.why: Accepting the old label is the clinical fail in this station.

avoid.dont: “Take these iron tablets and we’ll recheck in three months.”
avoid.instead: “I’ll start iron because you need it — and at the same time find out why you’re low.”
avoid.why: Treating the number without seeking the cause misses the diagnosis.

Thank you for saying that. It makes sense after years of feeling like this — and I don’t think you’ve been making a fuss over nothing. I think your body has been telling us something.
SCA_MODELS.why: Validates the fear and the self-sacrificing pattern

SCA_MODELS.text: Here’s what stands out. IBS doesn’t make people anaemic — and you are. Put that with the tummy symptoms, the tiredness, the mouth ulcers and the weight loss, and I think of a condition called coeliac disease, where the gut reacts to gluten and stops absorbing iron properly.
SCA_MODELS.why: IDA is a flag against IBS; names coeliac from the cluster

SCA_MODELS.text: Coeliac? I’ve had IBS for years. Nobody’s ever said that.

It’s common and it hides behind an IBS label for years. The good news is it’s a blood test to start with, and if it’s positive a specialist confirms it with a small sample from the gut taken during a camera test.
SCA_MODELS.why: Explains serology then biopsy confirmation in adults

SCA_MODELS.text: One thing matters more than anything else: the test only works if you keep eating gluten — bread, pasta, cereal in more than one meal every day. Please don’t cut it out before the test, or the result can come back falsely normal. Can you tell me back what I’ve asked you to do?
Keep eating bread and pasta as normal, don’t go gluten-free yet, even if I want to.

Exactly. So the plan I’d suggest: the coeliac blood test with a total antibody level, iron stores and a few other checks, and a stool test that looks for gut inflammation. I’ll also start iron now, because you need it — but alongside finding out why, not instead of it. How does that sound?
SCA_MODELS.why: Anaemia work-up plus treatment, not iron alone

SCA_MODELS.text: That makes sense. What about stronger tablets for my stomach?

I’d rather not escalate those yet — if this is coeliac disease, stronger tablets only mask it. Use your loperamide sparingly if you need it for school. If the test is positive, you’d see a gut specialist and a dietitian, and many people feel like a different person once they’re properly gluten-free.
SCA_MODELS.why: Negotiates the request honestly and offers hope

SCA_MODELS.text: That would be amazing. I’d love my energy back.
And while we wait, is there anything at work that would help — even just not taking on extra this term?
SCA_MODELS.why: Tailors the plan to her “no time to be ill” pattern

SCA_MODELS.text: Maybe. I always say yes to everything.

If you notice blood in your stools, black stools, weight dropping further, severe pain, or feeling breathless or faint, contact us sooner rather than waiting. I’ll book a call to go through the results in about two weeks.
SCA_MODELS.why: Specific safety-net and a booked follow-up

SCA_MODELS.text: Okay. Thank you — I came in for tablets and I feel like I’ve actually been listened to.
So: keep eating gluten, bloods and stool test this week, iron started, and a call in two weeks. Anything we haven’t covered?
No, that’s everything.

SCA_STEM.name: Erin Doyle
pmh: Long-standing “IBS” (bloating, loose stools, cramps) — clinical label, no documented work-up
SCA_STEM.recent: Bloods taken for tiredness: iron-deficiency anaemia. No coeliac serology on record. Teacher.
SCA_STEM.reason: Video consultation to discuss her blood results and her bowel symptoms.

SCA_KNOWLEDGE.guideline: NICE NG20 (2015) · NICE CG61 (2008, updated 2017) · NICE HTG320 (2013, formerly DG11) · BSG iron-deficiency anaemia guideline (2021)
SCA_KNOWLEDGE.summary: IBS does not cause iron-deficiency anaemia. Years of “IBS” plus iron deficiency, tiredness, mouth ulcers and a little weight loss is coeliac disease until serology says otherwise — tested correctly, while she is still eating gluten.

points.t: NICE CG61: IBS is diagnosed only after the red flags and baseline tests are clear — FBC, ESR/CRP and coeliac serology. Anaemia and unexplained weight loss are among the features that call for further investigation rather than an IBS label.

points.h: Who to test for coeliac disease
points.t: NICE NG20: offer serology to people with persistent unexplained GI symptoms, IBS-type symptoms, unexplained iron, B12 or folate deficiency, unexplained weight loss, prolonged fatigue, severe or persistent mouth ulcers, type 1 diabetes, autoimmune thyroid disease, and first-degree relatives of people with coeliac disease. A sister with type 1 diabetes adds weight to an autoimmune picture but is not in itself a testing criterion.

NICE NG20: first-line is total IgA plus IgA tissue transglutaminase (tTG-IgA); use IgG-based tests if IgA-deficient. The person must eat gluten in more than one meal every day for at least 6 weeks before testing. Advise explicitly not to cut gluten out before the diagnosis is confirmed.

NICE NG20: positive serology → refer to gastroenterology for endoscopic duodenal biopsy, still eating gluten. Do not diagnose coeliac disease in adults on serology alone. After diagnosis: lifelong gluten-free diet, dietitian support, bone health assessment, and assessment for functional hyposplenism with vaccination per the Green Book (pneumococcal where indicated).

points.h: The anaemia in its own right
points.t: BSG 2021: confirm iron deficiency with ferritin, screen all adults with IDA for coeliac disease, ask about menstrual loss and diet, and treat with oral iron while the cause is sought — product and dose per BNF. In premenopausal women, GI investigation is guided by symptoms, age and family history, and offers FIT to adults with iron-deficiency anaemia. Faecal calprotectin (NICE HTG320) helps separate IBD from IBS in adults with lower GI symptoms.

Untreated coeliac disease leads to ongoing malabsorption, anaemia, low bone density and subfertility, and rarely small-bowel lymphoma. A gluten-free diet usually settles symptoms and restores iron, so a named diagnosis is worth far more than stronger antidiarrhoeals.

SCA_SC_TASKS.d: Open question first; let her describe the “IBS”, the tiredness and what the anaemia result meant to her before responding to the tablet request.
Teaching workload, the impact of exhaustion on work and identity, and the “no time to be ill” pattern.
Picked up “not the person I was”, the weight loss she dismissed and the mouth ulcers she blamed on stress.
Her idea (long-standing IBS plus work), the buried fear that something is really wrong, and her wish for stronger tablets and iron.
Total IgA plus tTG-IgA while on gluten; ferritin and haematinics; ESR/CRP; faecal calprotectin; abdominal examination at a face-to-face review.
Coeliac disease versus IBD versus menstrual or dietary iron loss; recognises that IBS does not explain iron deficiency.
Asked about rectal bleeding, nocturnal symptoms and weight loss; clear on when this becomes urgent.
Possible coeliac disease under a long IBS label, with iron-deficiency anaemia from malabsorption — shared in plain words.
Keep eating gluten (more than one meal a day, at least 6 weeks); serology; oral iron while investigating; biopsy referral if positive; no escalation of antidiarrhoeals.
Looks for other deficiencies (B12, folate, vitamin D); plans dietitian, bone health and vaccination if coeliac is confirmed.
Results review booked; GI bleeding, further weight loss, severe pain or anaemia symptoms named for earlier contact.

social.t: A teacher who says yes to everything and has “no time to be ill”. Exhaustion is affecting her work and sense of self; the plan must fit a school timetable, not add guilt.
If confirmed, a lifelong gluten-free diet affects shopping, cost, eating out and school meals. Dietitian input and label-reading skills decide whether it works.

legal.t: If fatigue or investigations affect her work, a fit note can suggest adjustments (for example altered duties) rather than full absence. Coeliac disease can be a disability under the Equality Act 2010 where its effects are substantial and long-term — relevant only if symptoms persist.

professional.t: A diagnosis recorded years ago is a working hypothesis, not a fact. New results that don’t fit — iron deficiency here — are a prompt to re-examine it (GMC Good Medical Practice 2024: good clinical care).
Escalating antidiarrhoeals or giving iron without investigating the cause would treat numbers and symptoms, not the patient. Document the reasoning and the gluten advice.

community.t: Coeliac UK (information, food directory, local groups); community pharmacy for iron counselling; practice dietitian or local dietetic service after diagnosis. Gluten-free food on prescription varies by area.

redFlags: Iron-deficiency anaemia with bowel symptoms — not explained by IBS
Unintentional weight loss, rectal bleeding, nocturnal diarrhoea — investigate rather than label
Symptoms of significant anaemia: breathlessness, chest pain, near-faints — earlier review
psychosocial: Impact of fatigue on teaching and on how she sees herself
The “no time to be ill” pattern that has kept her normalising symptoms
Practical barriers to tests and to a future diet change
ice: Idea: “It’s my IBS and work tiredness”
Concern: a buried fear that something is really wrong, pushed down for years
Expectation: stronger tummy tablets and iron, quickly

SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosis: Be honest that the label may be wrong: “IBS doesn’t cause iron deficiency. With your symptoms, the ulcers and the weight loss, I want to test for coeliac disease — and I’d like to find the cause rather than keep treating the symptoms.”
SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosisLay: “Think of the lining of your gut as a thick carpet that soaks up iron and nutrients. In coeliac disease, gluten wears the carpet thin, so iron slips through. The blood test looks for the body’s reaction to gluten — which is why you need to keep eating it until we’ve tested.”

management.reflectIce: “You’ve been quietly worried something is really wrong and kept going anyway. I think you were right to wonder — and the good news is that what I’m looking for is very treatable.”
management.psychosocial: Work with her pace: one set of tests this week, iron started, a results call booked. Invite her to take something off her plate at work while this is sorted.
sharedPlan: Total IgA plus tTG-IgA while eating gluten in more than one meal a day (at least 6 weeks); ferritin, B12, folate, ESR/CRP; faecal calprotectin
Oral iron now, product and dose per BNF, while the cause is sought
Positive serology → gastroenterology for duodenal biopsy; dietitian, bone health and vaccination review if confirmed
safetyNet: Rectal bleeding or black stools, further weight loss, severe pain, breathlessness or faintness → contact the practice promptly
Results review in about two weeks; do not start a gluten-free diet until told the diagnosis is confirmed

SCA_PITFALLS.intro: This station is failed by doctors who treat the request rather than the patient: a stronger tablet, some iron, and a diagnosis nobody checked. The marks sit in spotting that the numbers don’t fit the label, and in testing correctly.

items.fail: Accepting “IBS” and prescribing a stronger antispasmodic or antidiarrhoeal.
items.why: IBS does not cause iron-deficiency anaemia; NICE CG61 requires anaemia and weight loss to be investigated. “Management plan not in line with current UK best practice.”
items.fix: Say it out loud: “IBS doesn’t make people anaemic — so I want to look for a cause.” Then test for coeliac disease.

items.fail: Suggesting a trial of gluten-free diet before any blood test.
items.why: NICE NG20: the person must eat gluten in more than one meal a day for at least 6 weeks before testing; going gluten-free makes serology and biopsy unreliable.
items.fix: Give the instruction clearly and check it with teach-back: “Tell me what I’ve asked you to do about bread and pasta.”

items.fail: Ordering tTG-IgA alone, or diagnosing coeliac disease on serology and starting the diet.
items.why: Total IgA is needed to avoid a false negative in IgA deficiency, and adults need biopsy confirmation (NICE NG20).
items.fix: “A blood test for the antibody and your total antibody level; if it’s positive, a specialist confirms it with a small sample from the gut.”

items.fail: Missing “I’m not the person I was” and moving straight to tests.
items.why: “Does not identify or respond to the patient’s cues.” Her hidden agenda is a long-suppressed fear, and it is what makes her engage with the plan.
items.fix: Pause: “Has part of you been wondering whether something more is going on?” Then validate before explaining.

items.fail: Dismissing her request flatly — “No, you don’t need stronger tablets.”
items.why: Refusing without explanation reads as paternalistic and loses her trust in the investigation plan.
items.fix: Explain why: “If this is coeliac disease, stronger tablets would only hide it. Let’s find the cause — and I’ll treat your iron today.”

items.fail: Closing with “we’ll ring you with the results” and nothing else.
items.why: Non-specific safety-netting and no defined follow-up are standard failing feedback.
items.fix: Name the red flags (bleeding, black stools, weight loss, faintness), book the results call, and summarise the plan in one sentence.
